title: Candidate keys and alternate keys
description: A practical guide to separating all possible row identifiers from the one identifier chosen as the primary key, using a hypothetical retail order table with counterexamples.
lead: A candidate key is any minimal set of attributes that can identify one row. The primary key is the candidate key the model chooses as the main identifier. Alternate keys are the candidate keys left over. The distinction matters because a table can have several legitimate identifiers, but only one should become the default target for references, joins, and downstream assumptions.

sections.heading: The short version
paragraphs: In relational modeling, a superkey is any set of attributes that uniquely identifies a row. A candidate key is a minimal superkey: it identifies a row, and no attribute can be removed without losing that identifying power. A primary key is the candidate key selected as the table’s main identifier. An alternate key is a candidate key that was not selected as the primary key.

The practical mistake is to call every unique-looking column a key. A column can appear unique in today’s extract and still fail as a candidate key because nulls are allowed, the value is only unique within a subset of rows, or the value is not part of the business rule for the relation. A key is a rule about the relation, not just a profile of one file.

For data engineers, the difference shows up in schema design, deduplication, dimensional modeling, and pipeline checks. If a model keeps only the primary key and ignores alternate keys, valid duplicate detection paths disappear. If it promotes a weak identifier to primary key, joins and foreign keys inherit the wrong grain.
bullets: Candidate key: a minimal identifier for every row in the relation.
Primary key: the candidate key chosen as the table’s main identifier.
Alternate key: a candidate key not chosen as primary.
Unique but not a candidate key: a value that happens to be unique in a sample, is nullable, applies only to some rows, or includes unnecessary columns.

sections.heading: A hypothetical retail order example
paragraphs: Consider a hypothetical retail order table. The table records one row per accepted order, regardless of whether the order came from a web shop, a store register, or a marketplace integration. The table includes an internal order_id and an order reference assigned by the channel that accepted the order.

The sample below is intentionally small. It is not proof of any key by itself. It is a fixture for reasoning about possible identifiers and counterexamples. The business rule we will assume is this: every order receives one internal order_id, and every order also receives a channel_order_ref that is unique only within its channel_code.

codeExamples.code:
WITH hypothetical_retail_order (
    order_id,
    channel_code,
    channel_order_ref,
    customer_id,
    receipt_no,
    payment_auth_code,
    submitted_at
) AS (
    VALUES
        (1001, 'web',         '50001', 'C-101', NULL,   'AUTH-701', TIMESTAMP '2026-09-01 09:15:00'),
        (1002, 'store',       '50001', 'C-102', 'R-88', 'AUTH-702', TIMESTAMP '2026-09-01 09:18:00'),
        (1003, 'web',         '50002', 'C-101', NULL,   'AUTH-703', TIMESTAMP '2026-09-01 09:22:00'),
        (1004, 'marketplace', '50001', 'C-103', NULL,   'AUTH-704', TIMESTAMP '2026-09-01 09:25:00'),
        (1005, 'store',       '50003', 'C-104', 'R-88', 'AUTH-705', TIMESTAMP '2026-09-01 09:29:00'),
        (1006, 'web',         '50004', 'C-105', NULL,   'AUTH-705', TIMESTAMP '2026-09-01 09:31:00')
)
SELECT *
FROM hypothetical_retail_order;

sections.heading: Classifying the identifiers
paragraphs: In this example, order_id is a candidate key if the relation’s rule says every order has exactly one non-null internal identifier and no two orders share it. It is minimal because order_id alone is enough; adding another column would create a larger superkey, not a better candidate key.

The pair (channel_code, channel_order_ref) is also a candidate key under the stated business rule. channel_order_ref alone is not enough because 50001 appears for web, store, and marketplace orders. channel_code alone is not enough because each channel has many orders. Together, the two attributes identify one order, and neither attribute can be removed. That makes the pair a minimal superkey, therefore a candidate key.

If the model chooses order_id as the primary key, then (channel_code, channel_order_ref) becomes an alternate key. It is still a real identifier. It should not disappear from the design just because it was not selected as primary. It may be the identifier used in source-system reconciliation, customer service lookup, or event ingestion from the ordering channel.

The set (order_id, channel_code) is a superkey but not a candidate key. It identifies each row because order_id already identifies each row. But it is not minimal: channel_code can be removed without losing uniqueness. This is a common source of confusion in wide analytical tables where many combinations are unique simply because they include an already-unique column.
bullets: order_id: candidate key, and likely primary key if selected as the main internal identifier.
channel_code plus channel_order_ref: candidate key, and an alternate key if order_id is the primary key.
channel_order_ref alone: not a candidate key because the same reference can occur in multiple channels.
order_id plus channel_code: superkey, not candidate key, because it is not minimal.

sections.heading: Counterexamples to common false keys
paragraphs: The same fixture shows why several tempting attributes are not candidate keys. customer_id is not an order identifier because the same customer can place multiple orders. In the sample, customer C-101 appears on orders 1001 and 1003. That is not a data quality problem; it is the expected relationship between customers and orders.

receipt_no is not a candidate key for the order relation. Some orders have no receipt number because they did not originate at a store register. The value R-88 also appears more than once in the hypothetical sample, which could happen if receipt numbers are reused by store, register, day, or another scope that is not represented in the column. The modeling lesson is not that receipts are useless. It is that receipt_no alone does not identify every order in this relation.

payment_auth_code is also not safe as a candidate key in this fixture because AUTH-705 appears on two rows. Even if a payment processor reference were unique in another model, it would identify a payment authorization, not necessarily an order. One order can have multiple payment events, and one payment event can be corrected, retried, voided, or associated with other operational records. The identifier must match the table’s grain.

A nullable unique column deserves special attention. In SQL implementations, a uniqueness constraint and a relational key are not always the same thing. A candidate key is an identifier for every tuple, so its attributes must be present for every row. If a supposed key can be null for valid rows, it is not a candidate key for that relation. It may be a conditional identifier for a subset, which should be modeled and named as such.

WITH hypothetical_retail_order (
    order_id,
    channel_code,
    channel_order_ref,
    customer_id,
    receipt_no,
    payment_auth_code,
    submitted_at
) AS (
    VALUES
        (1001, 'web',         '50001', 'C-101', NULL,   'AUTH-701', TIMESTAMP '2026-09-01 09:15:00'),
        (1002, 'store',       '50001', 'C-102', 'R-88', 'AUTH-702', TIMESTAMP '2026-09-01 09:18:00'),
        (1003, 'web',         '50002', 'C-101', NULL,   'AUTH-703', TIMESTAMP '2026-09-01 09:22:00'),
        (1004, 'marketplace', '50001', 'C-103', NULL,   'AUTH-704', TIMESTAMP '2026-09-01 09:25:00'),
        (1005, 'store',       '50003', 'C-104', 'R-88', 'AUTH-705', TIMESTAMP '2026-09-01 09:29:00'),
        (1006, 'web',         '50004', 'C-105', NULL,   'AUTH-705', TIMESTAMP '2026-09-01 09:31:00')
)
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count
FROM hypothetical_retail_order
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

WHERE receipt_no IS NOT NULL

sections.heading: A diagnostic framework for candidate keys
paragraphs: A data profile can disprove a candidate key, but it cannot prove one on its own. If a column has duplicates in valid rows, it is not a candidate key. If a column has no duplicates in the current extract, that only says the extract did not contain a counterexample. The candidate key decision still needs a business rule: what is the relation, what is its grain, and what values are guaranteed to exist?

Use four checks. First, check population: every attribute in the proposed key must be present for every row in the relation. Second, check uniqueness: no two valid rows can share the same full key value. Third, check minimality: remove one attribute at a time; if the remaining attributes still identify the row, the original set was only a superkey. Fourth, check scope: the identifier must apply to the table’s whole population, not only one source, one channel, or one lifecycle state.

The diagnostic query below is useful for finding current violations of a proposed key. It should be treated as a counterexample search, not as final proof. If it returns rows for (channel_code, channel_order_ref), the assumed alternate key is wrong or the data contains invalid duplicates. If it returns no rows, the next step is to confirm the rule with the source-system contract or domain owner.

codeExamples.code:
SELECT
    channel_code,
    channel_order_ref,
    COUNT(*) AS row_count
FROM hypothetical_retail_order
GROUP BY channel_code, channel_order_ref
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

SELECT
    COUNT(*) AS rows_missing_proposed_key_parts
FROM hypothetical_retail_order
WHERE channel_code IS NULL
   OR channel_order_ref IS NULL;

sections.heading: Implementing primary and alternate keys
paragraphs: A relational design should normally enforce both the selected primary key and the alternate keys that are part of the table’s meaning. If order_id is selected as the primary key, the alternate key on (channel_code, channel_order_ref) should still be represented with a uniqueness constraint and non-null constraints. This tells both humans and database tools that the channel identifier is not just descriptive text; it is another legitimate way to identify the same order.

The primary key choice is partly semantic and partly practical. A short stable internal identifier can be convenient for foreign keys, fact tables, and operational joins. A natural or source-system identifier can be more meaningful for reconciliation and debugging. The important point is that choosing one as primary does not demote the other into an ordinary attribute if it still satisfies the candidate key rule.

Here is a simplified PostgreSQL-style definition for the hypothetical order table. It uses order_id as the primary key and enforces the channel-level candidate key as an alternate key. This is a modeling example, not a performance recommendation.

codeExamples.code:
CREATE TABLE hypothetical_retail_order (
    order_id bigint PRIMARY KEY,
    channel_code text NOT NULL,
    channel_order_ref text NOT NULL,
    customer_id text NOT NULL,
    receipt_no text,
    payment_auth_code text,
    submitted_at timestamp NOT NULL,
    CONSTRAINT uq_hypothetical_retail_order_channel_ref
        UNIQUE (channel_code, channel_order_ref)
);

sections.heading: The decision rule
paragraphs: When reviewing a table design, list all plausible identifiers before naming the primary key. Then classify each one. Is it a candidate key for the entire relation? Is it merely a non-minimal superkey? Is it unique only for the current sample? Is it an identifier for a different entity? This prevents the primary key decision from hiding other important constraints.

For the hypothetical retail order table, the clean classification is: order_id and (channel_code, channel_order_ref) are candidate keys under the stated rules; order_id is selected as primary; (channel_code, channel_order_ref) is the alternate key; customer_id, receipt_no, and payment_auth_code are not candidate keys for this relation based on the counterexamples and grain mismatch.

The useful mental model is simple: candidate keys are the menu of valid identifiers. The primary key is the one chosen from that menu. Alternate keys are the valid choices that remain on the menu after the primary choice is made.

takeaways: Do not start by asking which column is the primary key. Start by listing every minimal identifier that could identify one row in the relation.
A primary key is a selected candidate key. Alternate keys are candidate keys that were not selected, and they often deserve explicit uniqueness constraints.
A data profile can find counterexamples to a proposed key, but the absence of duplicates in one extract does not prove a candidate key without a business rule.
Unique-looking attributes are not candidate keys if they are nullable for valid rows, apply only to a subset, include unnecessary columns, or identify a different entity.

title: Functional dependencies in analytical tables
description: A practical guide to using functional dependency violations to find attributes stored at the wrong grain in analytical tables.
lead: Functional dependencies are a useful diagnostic for analytical models because they make grain mistakes visible. If a column is supposed to describe an order, every row for that order should agree on its value. When the rows disagree, the table is telling you that the attribute is not actually stored at the grain you think it is, the determinant is incomplete, or the data is inconsistent.

sections.heading: Dependency violations as grain signals
paragraphs: A functional dependency says that one set of columns determines another column. In relational notation, X -> Y means that whenever two rows have the same X value, they must also have the same Y value. For example, if order_id -> order_date is true, then all rows with order_id O-1001 must have the same order_date.

In analytical work, this is most useful when the table is intentionally wider than a normalized transaction model. A line-level fact table may repeat order-level, customer-level, store-level, and product-level attributes for convenience. Repetition is not automatically a defect. The defect appears when the repeated attribute does not behave as if it belongs to the grain claimed by the model.

The practical question is not, “Is this table normalized?” It is, “Does this attribute vary at the same grain as the row, or is it being repeated from another grain?” Dependency checks are a compact way to answer that question. If the declared grain is one row per order line, then a true order-level attribute should be functionally dependent on order_id. A true product-level attribute should be functionally dependent on sku, assuming sku is the product identifier in that model. A true line-level attribute may vary by order_id and line_nbr together.

This article assumes you already know how to reason about identifiers and candidate keys. The focus here is narrower: using dependency violations to locate attributes that are stored at the wrong grain or described with the wrong determinant.

sections.heading: A hypothetical order-line table with counterexamples
paragraphs: Consider a hypothetical retail table called order_line_wide. Its intended grain is one row per order line. That means order_id and line_nbr together identify a line. The table also carries convenient descriptive columns such as loyalty_tier_at_order, ship_city, and product_category.
The following fixture is intentionally small and contains counterexamples. It is not a recommended model. It exists so the dependency checks have something concrete to find.
bullets: Expected order-level dependency: order_id -> loyalty_tier_at_order. If loyalty_tier_at_order means the customer’s tier at the time the order was placed, every line for the order should agree.
Questionable order-level dependency: order_id -> ship_city. This is true only if an order can ship to one city. If split shipments are allowed, ship_city is not order-grain.

Expected product-level dependency: sku -> product_category. This is true only if category is a stable attribute of the SKU in the reporting model. If categories are effective-dated or channel-specific, the determinant is incomplete.

codeExamples.code:
WITH order_line_wide AS (
  SELECT *
  FROM (VALUES
    ('O-1001', 1, DATE '2026-09-01', 'C-10', 'silver', 'S-10', 'Travel Mug',  'Drinkware', 'Seattle', 1),
    ('O-1001', 2, DATE '2026-09-01', 'C-10', 'gold',   'S-20', 'Tea Sampler',  'Grocery',   'Seattle', 2),
    ('O-1002', 1, DATE '2026-09-02', 'C-20', 'bronze', 'S-30', 'Desk Lamp',    'Home',      'Austin',  1),
    ('O-1002', 2, DATE '2026-09-02', 'C-20', 'bronze', 'S-40', 'Notebook Set', 'Office',    'Dallas',  3),
    ('O-1003', 1, DATE '2026-09-03', 'C-30', 'silver', 'S-10', 'Travel Mug',   'Kitchen',   'Boston',  1)
  ) AS t(
    order_id,
    line_nbr,
    order_date,
    customer_id,
    loyalty_tier_at_order,
    sku,
    product_name,
    product_category,
    ship_city,
    quantity
  )
)
SELECT *
FROM order_line_wide
ORDER BY order_id, line_nbr;

sections.heading: Querying for dependency violations
paragraphs: The basic diagnostic is simple: group by the determinant, count the number of distinct dependent values, and keep only groups with more than one dependent value. Each retained group is a counterexample to the proposed dependency.

The next query checks three proposed dependencies in the hypothetical table. It uses one common pattern repeatedly rather than relying on a special database feature. The query is written in a PostgreSQL-style form because the fixture uses a VALUES table expression and DATE literals; adapt syntax for other engines.

codeExamples.code:
WITH order_line_wide AS (
  SELECT *
  FROM (VALUES
    ('O-1001', 1, DATE '2026-09-01', 'C-10', 'silver', 'S-10', 'Travel Mug',  'Drinkware', 'Seattle', 1),
    ('O-1001', 2, DATE '2026-09-01', 'C-10', 'gold',   'S-20', 'Tea Sampler',  'Grocery',   'Seattle', 2),
    ('O-1002', 1, DATE '2026-09-02', 'C-20', 'bronze', 'S-30', 'Desk Lamp',    'Home',      'Austin',  1),
    ('O-1002', 2, DATE '2026-09-02', 'C-20', 'bronze', 'S-40', 'Notebook Set', 'Office',    'Dallas',  3),
    ('O-1003', 1, DATE '2026-09-03', 'C-30', 'silver', 'S-10', 'Travel Mug',   'Kitchen',   'Boston',  1)
  ) AS t(order_id, line_nbr, order_date, customer_id, loyalty_tier_at_order, sku, product_name, product_category, ship_city, quantity)
),
violations AS (
  SELECT
    'order_id -> loyalty_tier_at_order' AS dependency,
    order_id AS determinant_value,
    COUNT(DISTINCT loyalty_tier_at_order) AS distinct_dependent_values
  FROM order_line_wide
  GROUP BY order_id
  HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT loyalty_tier_at_order) > 1

  UNION ALL

  SELECT
    'order_id -> ship_city' AS dependency,
    order_id AS determinant_value,
    COUNT(DISTINCT ship_city) AS distinct_dependent_values
  FROM order_line_wide
  GROUP BY order_id
  HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT ship_city) > 1

  UNION ALL

  SELECT
    'sku -> product_category' AS dependency,
    sku AS determinant_value,
    COUNT(DISTINCT product_category) AS distinct_dependent_values
  FROM order_line_wide
  GROUP BY sku
  HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT product_category) > 1
)
SELECT *
FROM violations
ORDER BY dependency, determinant_value;

sections.heading: Reading the results without overreacting
paragraphs: The expected result has three violations. O-1001 has two loyalty_tier_at_order values. O-1002 has two ship_city values. S-10 has two product_category values. Each violation means the table contains rows that contradict the proposed dependency.

The first violation is a strong sign of a modeling or pipeline problem. If loyalty_tier_at_order is meant to describe the order, then it should not vary by line within O-1001. Possible causes include joining a current customer profile at different times, mixing historical and current customer attributes, or loading line rows from sources that applied different business rules. A better model might store the tier captured at order time in an order header table and repeat it into the line fact only through a consistent join. If the tier is actually recalculated per item promotion, then the column name is misleading and the determinant should include the line.

The second violation is different. It might reveal a bad value, but it might also reveal a wrong assumption. If the business allows one order to ship to multiple cities, then order_id -> ship_city is not a valid dependency. The column is not order-grain. It may be line-grain, shipment-grain, or allocation-grain. The fix is not to force all lines to share a city. The fix is to model the shipping concept at the grain where it truly varies, or rename the column to make its meaning explicit.

The third violation shows why dependency checks should lead to questions, not automatic refactors. If S-10 is a single product and product_category is supposed to be a stable product attribute, then S-10 appearing as both Drinkware and Kitchen is inconsistent. But if the business supports category changes over time, category by sales channel, or reporting taxonomy versions, then sku alone is not enough to determine product_category. The dependency might need sku plus effective_date, sku plus taxonomy_version, or sku plus sales_channel.

The diagnostic value comes from the counterexample. Instead of debating the whole table abstractly, you can point to a determinant value and ask, “Which row is right, or is our dependency wrong?” That is often the fastest route to discovering an attribute stored at the wrong grain.

codeExamples.code:
dependency                              determinant_value  distinct_dependent_values
order_id -> loyalty_tier_at_order        O-1001             2
order_id -> ship_city                    O-1002             2
sku -> product_category                  S-10               2

sections.heading: A practical diagnostic workflow
paragraphs: Use dependency checks as a short investigation loop. Start with the declared grain of the table, propose dependencies implied by that grain, then look for counterexamples. The goal is to classify each violation into one of a few actionable categories.

First, state the row grain in a sentence. For example: “One row per order line.” If the team cannot state the grain, dependency checks will still find oddities, but the results will be harder to interpret. Grain is the reference point that lets you distinguish a repeated order attribute from a true line attribute.

Second, list attributes that appear to come from another grain. In a line table, these often include order_date, customer_id, customer_tier, store_region, product_brand, product_category, campaign_name, and shipping address fields. For each one, write the determinant you believe should control it: order_id, customer_id, sku, store_id, campaign_id, or a composite determinant when the meaning requires it.

Third, query violations. Start with exact counts of distinct dependent values. Then inspect a few rows for each determinant value that fails. Counts tell you where to look; row samples tell you what kind of problem you have.
Fourth, classify the result. There are four common outcomes.
bullets: Data error: the dependency is valid, and one or more rows are wrong. Fix the source, transformation rule, or reference data mapping.
Wrong determinant: the attribute is valid, but the determinant is incomplete. Add the missing qualifier, such as effective date, channel, locale, taxonomy version, or shipment id.

Wrong grain: the attribute belongs to a different entity than the table suggests. Move it to the right dimension, header, bridge, snapshot, or child fact, then join or aggregate intentionally for reporting.
Acceptable denormalization: the attribute is repeated for analytical convenience, the dependency holds, and the repetition is understood. Document the dependency so future changes can be tested.

sections.heading: Limits and tradeoffs
paragraphs: A dependency violation is not proof of the correct design. It is proof that the proposed dependency does not hold for the data being checked. The next step is semantic: decide whether the data is wrong, the determinant is incomplete, or the attribute has been assigned to the wrong grain.

The reverse is also important: passing a dependency check does not prove the model is correct. A small dataset may simply not contain a counterexample yet. For example, a table may currently show one ship_city per order because no split shipment has occurred in the sample. That does not mean order_id -> ship_city is a safe business rule.

Null handling is another tradeoff. COUNT(DISTINCT column) behavior around nulls varies by database and may hide a pattern you care about. For dependency diagnostics, decide whether null means unknown, not applicable, not yet populated, or a real category. You may need separate checks for null presence as well as distinct non-null values.

Analytical models also intentionally duplicate data. A dimensional fact table may repeat descriptive attributes or join to dimensions for analyst convenience. Functional dependencies should not be used as a blunt rule that every repeated attribute must be removed. Use them to make grain assumptions testable. If a repeated attribute is intentional, stable, and documented, it may be perfectly reasonable in an analytical table.

The most valuable outcome is a short list of concrete counterexamples. A model review that says “customer attributes are mixed into the line fact” is easy to ignore. A model review that says “order O-1001 has two loyalty_tier_at_order values, and SKU S-10 has two product categories” gives the team something specific to resolve.

takeaways: Functional dependency checks turn grain assumptions into testable queries: group by the determinant and look for more than one dependent value.
A violation means the proposed dependency does not hold; it may indicate bad data, an incomplete determinant, or an attribute stored at the wrong grain.

Do not automatically normalize every repeated analytical attribute. Use dependency results to clarify semantics, document intentional denormalization, and move attributes only when their true grain requires it.

title: Composite keys in business event data
description: A practical guide to deciding when multiple columns together identify one business event, using a hypothetical retail POS event fixture with counterexamples and diagnostics.
primaryKeyword: Composite keys in business event data
relatedKeywords: Composite keys in business event data
lead: A composite key is not just a long identifier. In business event data, multiple columns identify one event only when the combination matches the event’s grain and survives realistic counterexamples. The practical question is: if two rows have the same values for these columns, are they the same business event, a duplicate observation, or two different events that happen to look similar?

sections.heading: Start with event identity, not with concatenation
paragraphs: The useful test for a composite key is semantic before it is technical. A set of columns identifies one event when equal values mean the same event within a declared population. That population matters. A receipt number may be unique inside one register on one business day, but not across all stores forever. A line number may be meaningful inside a receipt, but not by itself. A timestamp may be useful for ordering, but it is rarely enough to prove identity.

For this article, an event is a business occurrence that the model intends to count once: an item scanned, an item voided, a payment authorized, a subscription renewed, or a shipment dispatched. The event grain is the sentence that says what one row represents. For example: one row per point-of-sale event emitted by a register within a transaction. If the grain is unclear, the key discussion will drift into arguments about source quirks, deduplication, and downstream metrics.

The candidate key test has two parts. First, sufficiency: can two distinct events share the same proposed key values? If yes, the key is too small or the population is too broad. Second, minimality: can any column be removed while preserving the same identity guarantee? If yes, the key is larger than needed. Practitioners often skip the second test and create keys that include descriptive attributes such as SKU, amount, status, or customer ID. That can hide modeling errors because a correction to a descriptive attribute then appears to create a new event.

This article assumes the reader already knows the idea of candidate keys and alternate keys. The focus here is narrower: deciding whether several source columns, together, identify one business event in event-shaped data.

sections.heading: A hypothetical retail fixture with counterexamples
paragraphs: Consider the following hypothetical point-of-sale landing data. It is deliberately small and includes awkward cases that a clean diagram would hide. The intended business event is one register event inside one receipt transaction: opening the sale, scanning an item, voiding an item, or scanning a replacement item.

The fixture has a physical landing row identifier because files, streams, and ingestion jobs often need one. That identifier is not automatically the business event key. The question is whether the business columns identify the event.
bullets: landing_row_id is the physical row in the landing area.
store_id identifies the store.
register_id identifies the checkout register inside the store.
business_date is the store’s trading date, not necessarily the UTC date.
receipt_no is the receipt number assigned by the register.
event_seq is the register’s sequence number for events inside the receipt.
event_type describes what happened.
line_no is the receipt line affected by item-level events and is blank for transaction-level events.
sku, quantity, and amount are descriptive facts about the event, not presumed identifiers.

codeExamples.code:
WITH pos_events (
  landing_row_id,
  store_id,
  register_id,
  business_date,
  receipt_no,

sections.heading: Reject plausible keys with concrete counterexamples
paragraphs: The easiest way to find a composite key is to try to break it. Each proposed key should be challenged with a row pair that either already exists in the fixture or could reasonably exist under the same business rules.

Receipt number alone is not sufficient. Rows 1, 7, 8, and 9 all use receipt number 8841. They are not the same event. A receipt number is assigned within some operating scope. Without the store, register, and business date, the receipt number is only a local label.

Store plus receipt number is still not sufficient. Rows 1 and 8 show the same store and receipt number on different business dates. If receipt numbers restart daily, business_date is part of the transaction identity. Rows 1 and 7 show that register_id also matters if separate registers can produce the same receipt number.

Store, register, business date, and receipt number identify the transaction in this fixture, not the event. Rows 1 through 6 are all part of the same receipt transaction, but they are different business occurrences. A transaction key is a parent key. It is useful for grouping events, but it is not the event key.

Adding line_no does not solve the event identity problem. Row 3 scans SKU-B on line 2, row 5 voids line 2, and row 6 scans SKU-C on line 2 after the void. If the model used store_id, register_id, business_date, receipt_no, and line_no as the event key, it would collapse different events. It would also struggle with transaction-level events such as SALE_OPENED, where line_no is not applicable.

Adding event_type still may not be enough in a general design. In this fixture, store_id, register_id, business_date, receipt_no, line_no, and event_type separates the scan, void, and replacement scan shown here. But it relies on the assumption that the same event type cannot occur twice for the same receipt line. That assumption is often fragile. A cashier could scan the same SKU twice, a system could retry an authorization, or a promotion adjustment could be applied more than once. If the source emits an event sequence, that sequence is a stronger identity component than descriptive attributes.

The best candidate in this hypothetical fixture is store_id, register_id, business_date, receipt_no, and event_seq. It says: inside a store, register, business day, and receipt transaction, the register event sequence identifies the event. This key matches the source’s event-addressing scheme rather than the event’s descriptive contents.

Rows 3 and 4 are the important wrinkle. They have the same business key and the same descriptive values but different landing_row_id values. Under the declared grain, they are not two business events. They are duplicate observations of the same event, perhaps caused by a file replay or message redelivery. If the target table is one row per business event, rows 3 and 4 should not both survive as separate events. If the target table is one row per received message, then landing_row_id or another observation identifier belongs to that different grain.

sections.heading: Use diagnostics to separate key failure from duplicate observation
paragraphs: A uniqueness query can show whether a proposed key is unique in the data you have. It cannot, by itself, prove that the key is semantically correct. A dataset may be too small to contain the counterexample. That is why the diagnostic should be paired with business-scope questions: where does this number reset, what system assigns it, can the same event type repeat, and which columns are mutable descriptions?

The following illustrative SQL checks the proposed business event key in the hypothetical fixture. It reports rows that share the same event identity. In this data, the duplicate group is expected because rows 3 and 4 are duplicate observations of the same register event.

HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

sections.heading: A decision framework for composite event keys
paragraphs: Use the following decision path when deciding whether multiple columns together identify one event.

First, write the grain as a sentence. Avoid table names and source jargon. Good: one row per register event emitted within a receipt transaction. Weak: one row per POS record. If the sentence contains a parent concept such as order, receipt, session, or account, ask whether the row is the parent or an event within the parent.

Second, declare the key’s population. Is uniqueness expected across one source system, one tenant, one store, one device, one business date, or all time? Composite keys often exist because identifiers are locally unique, not globally unique. Leaving out the scope column creates accidental collisions. Adding an unnecessary global column can make the key harder to reason about.

Third, identify the source-assigned event address. In the fixture, event_seq is part of that address. In another system it might be event_id, sequence_number, message_offset within a partition, or a transaction-local attempt number. Prefer columns whose purpose is to address the event over columns that merely describe the event.

Fourth, remove descriptive and mutable attributes from the key unless the business rule truly defines identity by those values. SKU, amount, status, customer segment, and payment outcome are usually facts about the event. If a corrected amount changes the key, downstream tables may interpret a correction as a new event. That is a grain problem disguised as a key problem.

Fifth, treat nulls as a warning. A candidate key should not depend on a component that is sometimes not applicable, unless the population is split or the null has a well-defined identity meaning. SQL systems also have specific constraint behavior around nulls, so a uniqueness constraint may not enforce what the modeler intended. In relational design terms, primary keys identify tuples and should be non-null; implementation details vary by database system and constraint type.

Sixth, distinguish event identity from warehouse convenience. A warehouse may add a surrogate key for joins, compression, slowly changing dimensions, or tool compatibility. That does not eliminate the need to understand the natural or source-derived event key. The surrogate identifies a stored row; the composite business key explains why that row represents one event and supports deduplication, reconciliation, and constraint checks.

sections.heading: Common failure modes
paragraphs: One failure mode is using timestamps as identity. Timestamps are attractive because event tables always seem to have them. But two events can happen at the same recorded time, clocks can be coarse, and late-arriving corrections can carry the original event time. A timestamp can be part of an ordering or partitioning strategy without being part of the event key.

Another failure mode is using the parent key as the event key. An order_id may identify an order, not a payment attempt. A session_id may identify a session, not a page view. A receipt key may identify a transaction, not the scan, void, tender, and close events inside it. When counts look too low after deduplication, this is one of the first suspects.

A third failure mode is allowing ingestion identity to replace business identity. A Kafka offset, file row number, load UUID, or landing_row_id can identify an observation. That is valuable for lineage and replay handling. But if the same business event is delivered twice, observation identity alone will count it twice. Event models often need both: an observation key in the raw layer and a business event key in the conformed layer.

A final failure mode is building a composite key that is unique only because it includes every column. That is not a key; it is row fingerprinting. Fingerprints can help compare payloads, but they do not explain event identity. If changing quantity, price, or status changes the supposed key, the model cannot tell the difference between a new event and a corrected description of an existing event.

takeaways: Multiple columns identify one event only when equal values mean the same business occurrence within a declared population.
Test proposed composite keys with counterexamples: reset scopes, parent-versus-child grain, repeated event types, nullable components, mutable attributes, and duplicate observations.
Keep business event identity separate from physical row identity. Landing rows, file positions, and surrogate keys may be useful, but they answer different questions than the composite event key.

title: Natural keys versus surrogate keys
description: A practical guide to explaining identifier stability when a source system changes the identifier it previously used for the same business entity.
lead: The practical question in natural keys versus surrogate keys is not whether business identifiers are useful. They are. The question is what kind of promise each identifier can safely make. A source customer number may identify a customer in today’s extract, but that does not mean it is stable enough to be the long-lived identifier for every relationship in an analytical model. This guide uses a small hypothetical retail dataset to show how a source identifier can change, why that breaks a naive model, and how to separate business evidence from stable relational identity.

sections.heading: Identifier stability is not the same as identifier meaning
paragraphs: A natural key is a key whose values come from the business or source domain: an email address, SKU, employee number, policy number, account number, or source customer id. A surrogate key is a generated identifier with no business meaning inside the modeled domain. In practice, the important distinction is not meaningful versus meaningless. The important distinction is which identifier remains stable for the relationship you are modeling.

Assume the prerequisite idea of candidate keys: a table may have several column sets that uniquely identify rows. One candidate key can be chosen as the primary key; the others can be enforced as alternate keys. That does not automatically make every candidate key equally good for every relationship. A column can be unique at one point in the pipeline and still be a poor long-term reference for facts, dimensions, or downstream contracts.

Identifier stability asks a narrower question: if another table stores this value today, will that reference still point to the same intended entity after corrections, merges, splits, migrations, and source-system policy changes? If the answer is uncertain, the value may still be a useful alternate key, matching attribute, audit column, or source lineage field, but it should not carry the full burden of relational identity.
bullets: Meaning answers: does this value come from the business domain?
Uniqueness answers: does this value distinguish rows under a stated rule?
Stability answers: will this value continue to identify the same thing across time and change?
Relational identity needs the stability question, not just the meaning question.

sections.heading: A hypothetical retail counterexample: the source customer id changes
paragraphs: Consider a hypothetical retailer with online orders. The order feed includes a source_customer_id. At first glance, source_customer_id looks like a natural key for customers because the order system uses it to identify the customer. The data team builds customer and order tables that reference it directly.

Now introduce a common correction event: the source system merges a duplicate profile and changes the surviving customer id. The business still considers this one customer. Orders before the correction use the old id. Orders after the correction use the new id. The source also emits a change log showing that C-100 was replaced by C-901.
This example is intentionally small. It is not a benchmark, and it is not a claim about any particular retailer. It is a relational fixture for reasoning about key stability.

codeExamples.code:
-- Hypothetical source extracts

-- Customer profile extract on 2026-01-10
source_customer_id | customer_name | loyalty_tier
C-100              | Riley Chen   | Silver

-- Customer id change log emitted on 2026-02-01
old_source_customer_id | new_source_customer_id | changed_at   | reason
C-100                  | C-901                  | 2026-02-01   | duplicate profile merge

-- Order feed
order_id | ordered_at  | source_customer_id | order_total
O-10     | 2026-01-15  | C-100              | 72.00
O-11     | 2026-02-12  | C-901              | 35.00

sections.heading: What breaks when the changing source id is the primary key
paragraphs: If customer.source_customer_id is the primary key, there are two common failure modes. The first is duplication. The model inserts C-901 as a new customer because C-901 is a new primary key value. Historical order O-10 points to C-100, later order O-11 points to C-901, and customer-level reporting counts two customers unless every query knows how to collapse them.

The second failure mode is broken reference. The model updates the customer row from C-100 to C-901 but leaves historical orders untouched. Now order O-10 references C-100, which no longer exists in the customer table. A foreign key would reject this state; without a foreign key, the orphan may persist silently and appear as a missing customer in joins.

Both outcomes come from asking the source identifier to do two jobs at once. It is being used as source evidence and as the stable relational identity. When the source changes its identifier, those two jobs conflict.
bullets: Duplication failure: old and new source ids become two modeled customers even though the business correction says they are one.
Orphan failure: the customer table is updated to the new id, but older facts still reference the old id.
Query failure: every downstream query has to remember special merge logic instead of relying on a stable relationship.
Audit failure: after overwriting the old id, it becomes harder to explain what the source actually sent at the time of each event.

codeExamples.code:
-- Naive model: the source id carries stable identity.
-- This is the counterexample, not the recommended design.

CREATE TABLE customer_by_source_id (
  source_customer_id varchar(20) PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_name varchar(100),
  loyalty_tier varchar(20)
);

CREATE TABLE retail_order_by_source_id (
  order_id varchar(20) PRIMARY KEY,
  ordered_at date NOT NULL,
  source_customer_id varchar(20) NOT NULL,
  order_total numeric(10,2) NOT NULL,
  FOREIGN KEY (source_customer_id) REFERENCES customer_by_source_id(source_customer_id)
);

-- If the customer row is changed from C-100 to C-901,
-- order O-10 still contains C-100 and no longer has a valid parent.
-- If C-901 is inserted as a second customer, the same real customer is split.

sections.heading: Separate stable identity from source identifiers
paragraphs: A more stable design gives the modeled customer its own identifier and treats source customer ids as identifiers assigned by a particular source system during a particular period. This does not mean the source id is ignored. It means the source id is stored where its semantics are explicit.

In the hypothetical example, the modeled customer gets customer_sk 42. Both C-100 and C-901 map to customer_sk 42. Orders can store the raw source_customer_id for audit, but the resolved relational reference is customer_sk. The change log becomes evidence for maintaining the mapping, not a reason to rewrite the meaning of historical facts.

The suffix sk is often used for surrogate key, but naming is less important than the contract. The generated key must be stable for the modeled customer entity. In dimensional models, be careful not to confuse an entity-level durable key with a row-level surrogate key used for slowly changing dimension versions. A type 2 customer dimension may have many version rows for one customer. The fact table’s key choice should reflect the question: link to the customer entity, the customer version that was current at event time, or both.
bullets: Use the generated key as the relationship target when the source identifier can change.
Keep the source identifier as an alternate key, lineage attribute, or mapping row, not as the only identity.
Represent known changes explicitly instead of hiding them with destructive updates.
Let constraints enforce the contract where the relational engine can express it.

codeExamples.code:
-- Illustrative relational pattern for the hypothetical dataset.
-- Syntax is intentionally simple and may need adjustment for a specific SQL engine.

CREATE TABLE customer_entity (
  customer_sk bigint PRIMARY KEY,
  created_at date NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE customer_source_identifier (
  source_system varchar(50) NOT NULL,
  source_customer_id varchar(20) NOT NULL,
  customer_sk bigint NOT NULL,
  valid_from date NOT NULL,
  valid_to date,
  PRIMARY KEY (source_system, source_customer_id, valid_from),
  FOREIGN KEY (customer_sk) REFERENCES customer_entity(customer_sk)
);

CREATE TABLE retail_order (
  order_id varchar(20) PRIMARY KEY,
  ordered_at date NOT NULL,
  source_system varchar(50) NOT NULL,
  source_customer_id varchar(20) NOT NULL,
  customer_sk bigint NOT NULL,
  order_total numeric(10,2) NOT NULL,
  FOREIGN KEY (customer_sk) REFERENCES customer_entity(customer_sk)
);

-- Hypothetical resolved rows:
-- customer_entity
-- customer_sk | created_at
-- 42          | 2026-01-10

-- customer_source_identifier
-- source_system | source_customer_id | customer_sk | valid_from | valid_to
-- web_store     | C-100              | 42          | 2026-01-10 | 2026-02-01
-- web_store     | C-901              | 42          | 2026-02-01 | null

-- retail_order
-- order_id | ordered_at  | source_system | source_customer_id | customer_sk | order_total
-- O-10     | 2026-01-15  | web_store     | C-100              | 42          | 72.00
-- O-11     | 2026-02-12  | web_store     | C-901              | 42          | 35.00

sections.heading: Diagnostics for key churn
paragraphs: The simplest diagnostic is to compare source id change events with the identity mapping. If the source says old id C-100 and new id C-901 are the same customer, but the model maps them to different customer_sk values, the model has lost identifier stability.

A second diagnostic checks whether orders can be resolved through the mapping that was valid at order time. If orders cannot be resolved, either the mapping is incomplete, the validity dates are wrong, or the source emitted an identifier that the model does not know how to interpret.

These diagnostics are not a substitute for identity resolution policy. They only test whether the model is internally consistent with the evidence it has accepted. If email, phone, address, or device id are used as matching evidence, those rules need their own stewardship because they can also change, be shared, or be entered incorrectly.

codeExamples.code:
-- Hypothetical change log table.
-- A row says the source considers the old and new ids to be the same customer.

CREATE TABLE customer_id_change_log (
  source_system varchar(50) NOT NULL,
  old_source_customer_id varchar(20) NOT NULL,
  new_source_customer_id varchar(20) NOT NULL,
  changed_at date NOT NULL,
  reason varchar(100) NOT NULL
);

-- Diagnostic 1: source-declared id changes that map to different modeled customers.
SELECT
  c.source_system,
  c.old_source_customer_id,
  old_map.customer_sk AS old_customer_sk,
  c.new_source_customer_id,
  new_map.customer_sk AS new_customer_sk,
  c.changed_at
FROM customer_id_change_log c
JOIN customer_source_identifier old_map
  ON old_map.source_system = c.source_system
 AND old_map.source_customer_id = c.old_source_customer_id
JOIN customer_source_identifier new_map
  ON new_map.source_system = c.source_system
 AND new_map.source_customer_id = c.new_source_customer_id
WHERE old_map.customer_sk <> new_map.customer_sk;

-- Expected result for the hypothetical correct mapping: zero rows.

-- Diagnostic 2: orders whose raw source id cannot be mapped to a customer valid at order time.
SELECT
  o.order_id,
  o.ordered_at,
  o.source_system,
  o.source_customer_id
FROM retail_order o
LEFT JOIN customer_source_identifier m
  ON m.source_system = o.source_system
 AND m.source_customer_id = o.source_customer_id
 AND m.valid_from <= o.ordered_at
 AND (m.valid_to IS NULL OR o.ordered_at < m.valid_to)
WHERE m.customer_sk IS NULL;

-- Expected result for the hypothetical correct mapping: zero rows.

sections.heading: A decision rule for practitioners
paragraphs: The practical decision rule is: use a natural key as the primary relationship key only when it is unique, non-null, and stable for the lifetime of the relationships that will reference it. If it fails the stability test, keep it as an alternate key or source identifier and introduce a stable modeled key.

This does not make surrogate keys automatically correct. A generated key can be misused too. If the pipeline creates a new surrogate key every time the source id changes, it has merely converted source churn into surrogate churn. The generated key must be assigned at the grain of the intended entity and preserved when the accepted evidence says the entity is the same.

The tradeoff is that the stable-key design adds a mapping table and identity maintenance rules. That is extra modeling work. The benefit is that facts and dimensions can keep stable relationships while preserving the source values that arrived on each event. In analytical systems, that separation is often easier to reason about than pushing source correction logic into every downstream query.
bullets: Choose the relationship key based on stability, not on whether the value is natural or generated.
Use unique constraints for alternate keys when the business rule is enforceable, but do not confuse an alternate key with a durable relationship key.
Store raw source identifiers on events for audit and reconciliation.
Model identifier changes as data, especially when the source provides a merge, correction, or crosswalk feed.
Document what the stable key represents: a person, account, household, profile, customer version, or something else.

takeaways: A natural key can be meaningful and still be too unstable to serve as the long-lived relationship key.
When a source identifier changes for the same business entity, separate source evidence from modeled identity with a stable key and an identifier mapping.
A surrogate key only solves the problem if it is assigned at the correct grain and preserved across accepted source-id changes.
Diagnostics should check that source-declared id changes map to the same modeled entity and that events resolve through the valid identifier mapping.
Keep raw source identifiers for audit, but do not force every downstream query to reimplement identity correction logic.

title: Referential integrity across analytical tables
description: A practical guide to finding orphaned analytical facts while keeping legitimate late-arriving dimensions in the pipeline.
lead: Analytical systems often contain fact rows before every related dimension row has arrived. A strict inner join hides those facts. A strict orphan check may flag them too early. The practical problem is to separate true orphaned facts from facts that are only waiting for a late-arriving dimension.

sections.heading: The problem is not just missing rows
paragraphs: Referential integrity across analytical tables asks whether a fact row points to a valid dimension row. In an operational database, this may be enforced by a foreign key. In an analytical warehouse, the relationship is often enforced by pipeline logic, tests, and conventions instead. That does not make the relationship optional. It means the data team has to define what counts as valid and when to evaluate it.

The tricky case is timing. A retail order fact may arrive before the customer dimension record. If the customer record arrives tomorrow with an effective date that covers the order, the fact was not wrong. It was temporarily unresolved. Treating every missing dimension as a permanent orphan creates noisy alerts and can cause teams to drop usable revenue, order, or event records.

The inverse mistake is also common: using a simple left join to find missing dimension keys, then ignoring everything that has any matching customer identifier. That misses temporal mismatches, such as an order dated before the customer relationship was valid. Referential integrity for analytical tables usually needs both identity and time validity.

This article uses a hypothetical retail order dataset. The goal is not to introduce all dimensional modeling concepts. It is to build a small diagnostic that classifies facts into valid, pending late dimension, orphan missing dimension, orphan temporal mismatch, and invalid missing identifier.

sections.heading: A small hypothetical dataset with counterexamples
paragraphs: Assume a customer dimension is keyed by customer_id for this diagnostic. In a modeled warehouse, a fact might store a surrogate customer_key instead, but the same idea applies: choose the relationship that is supposed to prove the fact belongs to a valid dimension member. The prerequisite is that the dimension side has a candidate key or alternate key that the fact can reference unambiguously.

The dimension has a valid_from and valid_to range. The fact has an order_date and a fact_loaded_at date. The diagnostic runs as of 2026-09-23. The team allows a three-day grace period after fact_loaded_at before an unresolved customer is considered an orphan. That grace period is a business rule, not a universal law. Some pipelines may use one hour; others may use several days, depending on source latency and reporting needs.

The examples include five useful cases. O100 is valid. O101 was a late-arriving dimension case, but it is now valid because customer C002 exists with a validity range covering the order date. O102 is missing a customer dimension after the grace period, so it is an orphan. O103 is still inside the grace period, so it is pending rather than orphaned. O104 has no customer_id on the fact, so it is invalid for a different reason. O105 has a customer_id that exists, but not for the order date, so it is a temporal mismatch.

The important distinction is that the diagnostic does not decide whether to delete any fact. It classifies facts so downstream handling can be explicit. A reporting model might map pending rows to an unknown member, exclude only unresolved aged orphans from a certified metric, or publish an exception table for steward review.

codeExamples.code:
WITH
params AS (
  SELECT
    DATE '2026-09-23' AS as_of_date,
    INTERVAL '3 days' AS dimension_grace
),
dim_customer AS (
  SELECT *
  FROM (VALUES
    ('C001', DATE '2026-09-01', NULL,              DATE '2026-09-01'),
    ('C002', DATE '2026-09-01', NULL,              DATE '2026-09-22'),
    ('C005', DATE '2026-09-20', NULL,              DATE '2026-09-20')
  ) AS d(customer_id, valid_from, valid_to, dimension_loaded_at)
),
fact_orders AS (
  SELECT *
  FROM (VALUES
    ('O100', 'C001', DATE '2026-09-10', DATE '2026-09-10',  80.00),
    ('O101', 'C002', DATE '2026-09-15', DATE '2026-09-16', 120.00),
    ('O102', 'C004', DATE '2026-09-10', DATE '2026-09-10',  45.00),
    ('O103', 'C003', DATE '2026-09-22', DATE '2026-09-22',  60.00),
    ('O104', NULL,   DATE '2026-09-12', DATE '2026-09-12',  25.00),
    ('O105', 'C005', DATE '2026-09-10', DATE '2026-09-10',  35.00)
  ) AS f(order_id, customer_id, order_date, fact_loaded_at, amount)
),
classified AS (
  SELECT
    f.order_id,
    f.customer_id,
    f.order_date,
    f.fact_loaded_at,
    f.amount,
    CASE
      WHEN f.customer_id IS NULL THEN 'invalid_missing_customer_id'
      WHEN EXISTS (
        SELECT 1
        FROM dim_customer d
        WHERE d.customer_id = f.customer_id
          AND f.order_date >= d.valid_from
          AND (d.valid_to IS NULL OR f.order_date < d.valid_to)
      ) THEN 'valid'
      WHEN p.as_of_date < f.fact_loaded_at + p.dimension_grace THEN 'pending_late_dimension'
      WHEN EXISTS (
        SELECT 1
        FROM dim_customer d
        WHERE d.customer_id = f.customer_id
      ) THEN 'orphan_temporal_mismatch'
      ELSE 'orphan_missing_dimension'
    END AS integrity_status
  FROM fact_orders f
  CROSS JOIN params p
)
SELECT *
FROM classified
ORDER BY order_id;

sections.heading: How to read the classification
paragraphs: The diagnostic has a deliberate order. It checks for a missing fact identifier first, because a null or absent reference is not the same problem as an unmatched reference. It then checks whether a valid dimension row exists for the order date. If so, the fact is valid even if the dimension arrived after the fact. That is the key step that preserves legitimate late dimensions.

Only after the valid match fails does the grace period matter. O103 has customer C003, which is not in the dimension. Because the fact loaded on 2026-09-22 and the diagnostic runs on 2026-09-23 with a three-day grace period, the row is pending. It should be visible to operations, but it should not be counted as a true orphan yet.

O102 loaded on 2026-09-10. By 2026-09-23, the grace period has expired. No customer C004 exists, so the row is an orphan_missing_dimension. O105 is different. Customer C005 exists, but only from 2026-09-20 onward. An order on 2026-09-10 does not fall inside the customer dimension’s valid range, so the row is an orphan_temporal_mismatch. A join that only checks customer_id would incorrectly treat O105 as valid.

A compact expected result for the fixture is: O100 valid; O101 valid; O102 orphan_missing_dimension; O103 pending_late_dimension; O104 invalid_missing_customer_id; O105 orphan_temporal_mismatch. These labels are more useful than a single pass or fail result because each label suggests a different operational response.
bullets: valid: the fact has a matching dimension row for the relevant business date.
pending_late_dimension: the fact is unresolved, but still within the allowed arrival window.
orphan_missing_dimension: the grace period expired and no dimension row exists for the referenced identifier.
orphan_temporal_mismatch: the identifier exists, but not for the fact’s business date.
invalid_missing_customer_id: the fact lacks the identifier needed to evaluate the relationship.

sections.heading: Counterexamples: checks that look right but lose information
paragraphs: The first tempting pattern is to inner join facts to dimensions and publish only the joined rows. That produces clean-looking output, but it silently removes O102, O103, and O104. It may also hide O105 if the join ignores effective dates. Silent loss is dangerous because the published metric no longer reconciles to the fact intake. The team sees fewer bad rows, but only because the query discarded them.

The second tempting pattern is a left join anti-join with no grace period. That finds unresolved facts, but it treats O103 as an orphan immediately. If the source system commonly sends customer records after events, this creates false positives and alert fatigue. A useful integrity check must encode the expected latency window.

The third tempting pattern is a join on identifier only. That treats O105 as valid because C005 exists somewhere in the dimension. If the dimension represents history, the relationship should usually be evaluated at the fact’s business date. The exact date column depends on the process being modeled: order date, shipment date, event timestamp, policy effective date, or another domain-specific point in time.

A final caution is to avoid using the diagnostic query as the only place where business meaning lives. If the grace period, effective-date rule, and exception labels matter, put them where the pipeline and data consumers can find them: a test definition, a data contract, a model description, or an exception table specification.

codeExamples.code:
-- Counterexample 1: silently drops unresolved facts.
SELECT f.order_id, f.amount, d.customer_id
FROM fact_orders f
JOIN dim_customer d
  ON d.customer_id = f.customer_id;

-- Counterexample 2: flags every unresolved fact immediately,
-- even when the dimension may legitimately arrive within the grace window.
SELECT f.order_id, f.customer_id
FROM fact_orders f
LEFT JOIN dim_customer d
  ON d.customer_id = f.customer_id
WHERE d.customer_id IS NULL;

-- Counterexample 3: ignores whether the dimension was valid on the fact date.
SELECT f.order_id, f.customer_id
FROM fact_orders f
JOIN dim_customer d
  ON d.customer_id = f.customer_id;

sections.heading: A practical pattern for analytical pipelines
paragraphs: A durable implementation usually separates detection from policy. Detection classifies every fact. Policy decides what to do with each class. This keeps the warehouse from confusing data quality with data deletion.

For example, a daily model can write an order_integrity_exceptions table containing only pending_late_dimension, orphan_missing_dimension, orphan_temporal_mismatch, and invalid_missing_customer_id rows. A certified revenue model can include valid rows and optionally map pending rows to an unknown customer member, depending on reporting requirements. A reconciliation model can still sum all ingested facts so finance or operations can see the difference between intake totals and certified dimensional totals.

The grace period should be measured from a timestamp that reflects when the unresolved fact became visible to the analytical pipeline. In the fixture, that is fact_loaded_at. Measuring from order_date would be wrong if a source sends a week of historical facts in one batch; those facts would be marked orphaned before the dimension pipeline had a chance to process them. If the warehouse has separate source_created_at, source_updated_at, ingested_at, and modeled_at columns, choose the one that matches the service-level expectation being enforced.

The same pattern applies when facts store surrogate keys. If the fact uses a placeholder unknown key until the dimension is resolved, the diagnostic can evaluate the original source identifier retained on the fact or in a staging table. If the original identifier is not retained anywhere, distinguishing a legitimate late dimension from a true orphan becomes much harder. The model may still be queryable, but the integrity question has lost evidence.

One more design choice is whether late-arriving dimensions should repair old facts by updating a surrogate key, inserting a new version, or resolving at query time. That is a modeling policy. The integrity diagnostic remains the same in spirit: identify facts whose referenced dimension member is valid for the business date, facts that are still within the waiting period, and facts that failed after the waiting period.
bullets: Classify before filtering, so no fact disappears without a status.
Use a business-date validity check when the dimension represents history.
Apply a grace period before calling an unresolved relationship an orphan.
Keep pending and orphaned rows observable in an exception table or quality report.
Retain the source identifier needed to re-evaluate late-arriving dimensions.

sections.heading: A decision framework for the orphan check
paragraphs: Use the following sequence when defining referential integrity across analytical tables. First, name the relationship: which fact column references which dimension candidate key or surrogate key? Second, name the relevant business date used to test dimensional validity. Third, decide which load timestamp starts the waiting clock. Fourth, choose the grace period. Fifth, decide how each status affects published models.

The framework is intentionally relational rather than performance-oriented. A warehouse may implement it with constraints, SQL tests, orchestration checks, semantic model validations, or data observability tooling. The semantics should be the same even if the implementation changes.

The final test is whether the classification creates useful action. Pending rows ask, 'Did the related dimension arrive yet?' Orphan missing-dimension rows ask, 'Did the source send an impossible identifier, or did the dimension pipeline miss a row?' Temporal mismatches ask, 'Is the effective dating wrong, or did the fact reference the wrong business date?' Missing identifiers ask, 'Is the fact extract incomplete?' Those are different questions, so they deserve different labels.

takeaways: Do not use an inner join as an integrity check; it can hide the very facts that need investigation.
A late-arriving dimension should be considered valid once a dimension row exists for the fact’s relevant business date, even if the dimension loaded after the fact.
Classify unresolved facts with a grace period so pending late dimensions are not confused with true orphaned facts.
Check temporal validity when the dimension carries history; matching the identifier alone may be insufficient.
Keep exception statuses visible so downstream models can choose explicit handling instead of silently discarding data.
